title: Exploring the Biocompatibility and Therapeutic Potential of Graphene Oxide-Based Nanomaterials in Modern Medicine. A Comprehensive Review
abstract: Abstract Graphene oxide, a 2D nanomaterial, has attracted significant attention for biomedical applications due to its exceptional properties, including tunable surface chemistry, excellent dispersibility, and abundant oxygen-containing functional groups that facilitate facile modification. Recent advancements in the synthesis and functionalization of graphene oxide-based materials have addressed their limitations, such as poor solubility and cytotoxicity, thereby making them safer and more effective for biomedical applications. This paper thoroughly outlines the structural attributes and principal qualities of graphene oxide-based materials, highlighting their mechanical strength, thermal stability, impermeability, electrical conductivity, and biological properties. Emerging developments in graphene oxide-based nanocomposites for fluorescence imaging, magnetic resonance imaging, photoacoustic imaging, Raman spectroscopy imaging, and multifunctional therapeutic platforms are thoroughly examined. Their effectiveness in biomedical scaffolds, wound-healing systems, controlled drug-release platforms, and antimicrobial coatings has been highlighted. Notwithstanding considerable advancements, issues related to cytotoxicity, biodegradability, long-term biosafety, and scalable production continue to impede broad clinical translation. This study offers a cutting-edge overview of graphene oxide-based biomedical systems and outlines promising pathways for advancing safer, more effective, and clinically relevant graphene-based healthcare technologies.

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: In modern medicine, the treatment of complex diseases such as cancer, neurodegenerative disorders [ 1 ], and chronic wounds [ 2 ] presents significant challenges. Traditional therapies often suffer from issues such as non-specific drug delivery, high toxicity, and poor targeting of affected cells [ 3 ]. As a result, there is an increasing need for innovative therapeutic strategies that can overcome these limitations and provide more effective, targeted treatments. Globally, chronic wounds, including diabetic ulcers and venous ulcers, have become more prevalent with the aging population and rising incidences of chronic diseases like diabetes and vascular diseases. For example, the prevalence of chronic leg ulcers is estimated at 1.51 per 1000 population [ 4 ]. Similarly, chronic wounds, particularly pressure ulcers, are notably more common in elderly populations, with the incidence increasing significantly with age [ 5 ]. These wounds not only result in considerable medical expenses but also cause prolonged suffering and loss of function, contributing to a reduced standard of living.

The graphene oxide (GO) family of materials has recently garnered significant interest due to its wide range of potential applications in the biomedical industry [ 6 ]. Due to its two-dimensional (2D) carbon structure, graphene oxide (GO) exhibits exceptional mechanical strength, a large surface area, and functional groups that facilitate surface modification [ 7 ,  8 ]. The remarkable electron-transport properties and extensive interfacial contact area of graphene oxide substantially improve photocatalytic performance by facilitating charge-carrier separation and minimizing recombination losses in hybrid nanocomposites [ 9 ,  10 – 11 ]. Graphene oxide has been used in different fields of biomedicine, such as drug transport, bioimaging, tissue engineering, and cancer treatment [ 12 ]. The biomedical potential of GO has been largely driven by its remarkable versatility. It may be modified to produce biocompatible composites for targeted drug delivery and gene therapy, given the abundance of oxygen-containing groups, such as hydroxyl, carboxyl, and epoxy, on its surface. According to research, GO may be used as a vehicle for many medicinal substances, allowing for regulated release while reducing the negative effects of traditional pharmaceuticals [ 13 ]. Targeting molecules can be attached to functionalized GO, thereby improving its specificity for diseased cells, especially in cancer therapies. Furthermore, it is used in bioimaging as a contrast agent in magnetic resonance imaging [ 14 ] and fluorescence imaging [ 15 ].

Synthesis and functionalization of GO have recently made significant advancements in addressing some of the challenges associated with its biomedical applications. Traditionally, poor solubility and potential cytotoxicity have limited its use. However, recent research has led to the development of safer and more effective methods to enhance its water solubility and biocompatibility. Non-toxic reducing agents have been explored to produce reduced graphene oxide (rGO), which exhibits improved dispersibility in aqueous environments while maintaining its desirable properties for drug delivery and imaging applications [ 16 ]. The biodegradability of GO is also a critical factor in its long-term medical applications. Recent studies have shown that GO can degrade in the human body via specific enzymes, providing a safer alternative to other nanomaterials that may accumulate in tissues [ 17 ]. This biocompatibility and degradability make GO a promising candidate for a variety of clinical applications, including wound healing and the treatment of neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s, where GO nanocarriers can help reduce amyloid-beta toxicity [ 18 ].

The reviews that do cover graphene oxide (GO) functionalization in the context of biomedical application obstacles do so in a limited scope. Most reviews on GO cover the basic scientific properties, methods, and broad applications in drug delivery, tissues engineering, and other areas in biomedical engineering. However, most of these reviews ignore GO’s toxicity, biocompatibility, and possible controlled degradation in biological systems. While these reviews speak of GO’s great potential, they fail to recognize GO’s limitations in clinical applications, notably safety and efficacy. This paper attempts to address and focus on GO functionalization to address biocompatibility and limit potential toxicity. While there is literature available in the theoretical aspect of GO, the current paper will discuss the possible and practical aspects of GO. Further, new theoretical concepts to limit immunological response and accumulation of GO in tissues will be discussed. This research will focus on the safe utilization of GO and will focus on the available clinical applications for the treatment of chronic wounds, cancer, and other complicated pathologies. Unlike other research papers that consider GO to be a universal solution, this research will consider the limitations of GO in various biomedical applications and will also address the issues of surface modification and GO functionalization to limit toxicity.

Our review offers a broad, multi-domain overview of GO-based nanomaterials across modern medicine (bioimaging, drug/gene delivery, tissue engineering, wound healing, antimicrobial coatings, and biosensing), whereas the chapter is narrowly focused on cancer theranostics (imaging + PTT/PDT/drug delivery in oncology) [ 19 ]. We provide deeper, updated analysis of biocompatibility, enzymatic biodegradability, functionalization strategies for toxicity reduction, and recent first-in-human/large-animal safety data, with dedicated emphasis on long-term implantation risks.

sections.heading: Structure of Graphene Oxide
paragraphs: Carbon-based nanomaterials, especially graphene and its derivatives, have emerged as promising substances due to their exceptional structural, electrical, and thermal properties, facilitating various applications in biomedicine [ 20 ]. Extensive experimental investigations of the GO structure have been carried out over the years, utilizing various methods such as ultra-high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, X-ray diffraction,  13 C and  1 H nuclear magnetic resonance, and annular dark-field imaging [ 21 ,  22 ,  23 – 24 ]. Multiple efforts to explain the structure of graphene oxide have yielded competing structural models. The primary reasons for this are the complexity of the material and the uniqueness of each sample resulting from its variable stoichiometry. A combination of sp 2  and sp 3  hybridized carbon atoms is produced when graphene oxide monolayer sheets of graphite are functionalized with hydroxyl, carboxyl, and epoxy oxygen groups on both the basal plane and the edges [ 25 ]. Numerous GO models have been developed based on various studies and theoretical calculations. In their first proposal from 1939, Hofmann and Rudolf envisioned a graphite monolayer with many epoxy groups distributed at random [ 26 ]. In 1946, Ruess modified the structural model of graphene oxide by incorporating hydroxyl groups and suggesting a partial transformation of sp 2 -hybridized carbon atoms into sp 3 -hybridized carbon atoms [ 27 ]. Subsequently, Scholz and Boehm proposed a less-organized structure, lacking ether oxygen groups, characterized by undulating carbon layers that incorporate hydroxyl and carbonyl functionalities, as well as repeating C–C single bonds [ 28 ]. Additionally, in 1994, Nakajima and Matsuo developed a model that closely resembled a graphite intercalation compound [ 29 ]. The LK model proposed by Lerf and Klinowski consists of two distinct regions: one containing six-membered aliphatic rings and the other containing nonoxidized aromatic benzene rings [ 22 ].

The extent to which the material has been oxidized determines the relative sizes of the two zones. Adorned with epoxide groups and double bonds, the model is mostly composed of aromatic molecules. The hydroxyl groups bound to carbon atoms produce a slightly warped tetrahedral arrangement that leads to the wrinkling of the monolayer. Both the top and bottom carbon monolayers have oxygen functional groups attached, forming two layers of oxygen atoms with different proportions of epoxide and hydroxyl groups, closely packed together. Across the carbon monolayer, aromatic compounds and oxidized rings are present. The acidity of GO is caused by the presence of hydroxyl and carboxyl groups at the lattice surfaces. The LK model is a widely recognized representation of graphene oxide with a moderate oxidation state. Graphene oxide and its derivatives have become the focus of researchers worldwide since their discovery. The 2006 model by Szábó and Dékány, derived from an analysis of prior models, excluded carboxylic acids and comprised two principal components: cyclohexane chairs linked by 1,3-epoxide and intermediate alcohols, and corrugated hexane ribbons interspersed with quinones and ketones. Unlike the static LK model, the dynamical structural model proposed by Dimiev, Alemany, and Tour in 2013 [ 30 ] described the formation of different carbon structures containing bound water. Liu et al. recently provided experimental proof of C = O bonding at the carbon monolayer edge, which serves as the foundation for prior theories, notably the LK model [ 31 ,  32 ]. Graphene oxide comprises topological defects such as pentagons, heptagons, and octagons, as well as structural faults comprising adatoms, vacancies, and adsorbed pollutants.

Moreover, oxidation in the presence of concentrated acids facilitates the generation of oxidation byproducts, comprising low-molecular-weight oxidized carbon particles [ 33 ,  34 ]. Various oxidation byproducts, including highly oxidized polyaromatic particles and less oxidized GO platelets, are attached due to hydrogen bonding, π-π stacking, and van der Waals interactions [ 35 ]. Longer reactions of graphite with concentrated acids result in more oxidation debris [ 36 ,  37 ]. These fragments cannot be removed without first doing a base wash [ 37 ,  38 – 39 ]. In terms of oxidation level, pure GO, which does not include any oxidation residues, is on par with chemically reduced GO [ 40 ]. Kim et al. reported a two-step thermal method for the synthesis of hierarchically porous graphene. Initially, graphene oxide (GO) underwent annealing at 650 °C in an atmospheric environment, resulting in the decomposition of oxygen functionalities that emitted CO 2 /CO and expanded the sheets into slit nanopores, producing activated reduced graphene oxide (ArGO). A subsequent annealing at 600 °C in nitrogen eliminated residual oxygen groups and produced more micropores, yielding thermally treated ArGO [ 41 ]. sections.heading: Methods for Graphene Oxide Synthesis
paragraphs: Among the several permanganate techniques developed by Hummers and Offeman, the most commonly used and effective in the past is the Hummers method, as shown in Fig.  2 (a). Producing graphene oxide with this method is a rather quick example of classical technology [ 47 ]. A small amount of sodium nitrate, sulfuric acid, and potassium permanganate is the component of the reaction mixture. Between eight and twelve hours is the typical response time. Because it does not involve the creation of explosive ClO 2 , this method is much safer. After everything is finished, a diluted H 2 O 2  solution is used to neutralize the excess potassium permanganate. The carbon-to-oxygen ratios of BR-GO (2.2) and Hummers’ graphene oxide (2.25) are quite comparable. The method’s production of nitrogen oxides makes it harmful to the environment. Low- and room-temperature methods, as well as nitrate-free two-step and co-oxidant variations, are among the many modified Hummers’ processes available [ 48 ,  49 ,  50 ,  51 – 52 ].

In 1859, while investigating the reactivity of flake graphite, British scientist B. C. Brodie synthesized graphite oxide for the first time, as shown in Fig.  2  (b) [ 56 ,  57 ]. The oxidizing agent used in this chlorate route is potassium chlorate. Benjamin Brodie used a wide variety of strong oxidizing chemicals to finally uncover graphite’s structure. In the experiment, Brodie heated graphite with a mixture of fuming nitric acid and potassium chlorate at 60 °C for 4 days to produce BR-GO, or graphene oxide. His extensive series of oxidative treatments (4–7) yielded a C 11 H 4 O 5  formula, corresponding to a C/O ratio of 2.2, according to his calculations [ 57 ]. Product solubility in pure water was confirmed; nevertheless, flocculation in an acidic environment was observed. Brodie called it “graphic acid” since it didn’t react much with litmus paper. One such way to make chlorate is via the Staudenmaier process, as shown in Fig.  2  (c) [ 58 ]. In order to alter the chlorate addition method, Staudenmaier used sulfuric acid in the mixture. The risk of heat production and the formation of explosive by-products was reduced by gradually adding potassium chlorate to the mixture. The reaction time was shortened due to the increased acidity of the air [ 59 ]. The oxidation level of graphene oxide increases as the concentration of nitric acid decreases.

sections.heading: Advanced Methods of Graphene Oxide Synthesis
paragraphs: It is possible to produce graphite oxide and graphene oxide using a variety of ways. The standard procedure involves exposing the material to an acidic atmosphere and then oxidizing it. Two further possibilities are microbiological and electrochemical approaches. Tour’s graphene oxide process is classified as a permanganate method shown in Fig.  2  (d) [ 60 ]. In an ice bath, a 6:1 ratio of graphite to potassium permanganate is introduced, while a 1:9 ratio of phosphoric acid to sulfuric acid is combined. Stir the mixture for 12 h after heating it to 50 °C. After the mixture has cooled, it is spread over the ice. To remove the excess potassium permanganate, 30% H 2 O 2  is then added. Phosphoric acid acts as an etching agent, a dispersant, and an oxidation stabilizer, ensuring the safe synthesis of graphene oxide. This approach yields graphene oxide with a greater oxidation level and a more uniform structure.

Modern methods for oxidizing graphite to GO include chlorate and permanganate procedures, but also employ potassium chromate using nitric or perchloric acid, or to do the experiment using Jones’s conditions [ 61 ,  62 ]. Another, less dangerous option for making graphene oxide is to combine potassium ferrate with sulfuric acid [ 63 ]. While these results are encouraging, another study shows that GO synthesized using potassium ferrate is impossible [ 64 ]. Also, at 50 °C using Fe(VI) as a catalyst, graphite may be oxidized in water with H 2 O 2  with benzoyl peroxide at 110 °C [ 65 ,  66 ]. There is little change in the final product when the reaction time is cut in half, from 12 h to 1, according to Jankovský et al., who modified Tour’s technique [ 67 ]. Electrochemical synthesis provides an alternate way to chemical techniques for synthesizing graphene oxide, which could be crucial for industrial-scale production. Due to its reduced equipment cleaning requirements and ability to reuse the electrolyte, electrochemical manufacturing is preferable to chemical production from an environmental sustainability standpoint [ 68 ,  69 ]. One possible explanation for electrochemical graphene oxide’s (EGO) higher quality than traditional techniques is that it uses aqueous electrolytes and doesn’t employ oxidizing agents, which eliminates impurities [ 69 ]. It is also possible to control oxidation levels and fault density because of the variety of experimental setups.

sections.heading: Properties of Graphene Oxide-Based Composites
paragraphs: Graphene-based materials demonstrate distinctive physical, chemical, and biological properties, making them attractive for various applications. Their performance is closely associated with vital characteristics, including thermal stability, impermeability, mechanical strength, biocompatibility, and electrical conductivity, that are examined in this section. A comprehensive grasp of these features establishes the basis for assessing their suitability for use in biomedical technologies [ 70 ].

sections.heading: Mechanical Properties
paragraphs: 2D planar sheets of sp 2  hybridized carbon atoms organized in a hexagonal lattice, marked by very strong covalent bonds, make up perfect graphene as shown in Fig.  3  (a). The remarkable slippery elastic behavior and nonlinear properties of graphene are well-documented. When the inherent strength reaches a critical stress level of around 130 GPa, damage starts to occur [ 71 ]. The structural features of graphene give it remarkable mechanical capabilities, which contribute to its reputation as an extraordinarily strong material. One further thing that makes graphene perfect for electronics and high-performance sensors is its ability to be flexible. According to a study, the elastic modulus of GO paper is 32 GPa, and the break strengths are around 80 MPa [ 72 ].

The small amount of graphene in the polymer matrix gives GBC its remarkable mechanical properties, including increased tensile strength and elastic modulus. Graphene derivative (graphene’s inherent properties), loading value, polymer type, and technique all play important roles in the enhancement [ 77 ,  78 – 79 ]. Several tests have shown that adding graphene filler to the GBC significantly improves its mechanical properties. The mechanical properties of graphene–polymer composites typically enhance with higher graphene concentration until an optimal concentration is reached, after which filler aggregation results in performance decline [ 80 ]. Bao et al. examined two composites formulated with a PVA matrix incorporating 0.8 wt% graphene and 0.8 wt% reduced graphene oxide (rGO), respectively, and reported that the rGO/PVA composite demonstrated much superior mechanical abilities [ 81 ]. The findings demonstrate that rGO/PVA significantly enhanced mechanical characteristics when compared to GO/PVA. In comparison to GO/PVA, which showed gains of 54% in tensile strength and 52% in elastic modulus, rGO/PVA showed an increase of 66% in both metrics. Theoretically, this was due to the greater mechanical strength of rGO. Graphene oxide is an excellent addition for polymers because to its functional groups, which enhance mechanical characteristics, facilitate load transfer and interfacial interactions, and display good dispersion inside the polymer [ 78 ]. Furthermore, the method affects the ultimate composite characteristics in the opposite way. Specifically, 1 weight% rGO/PMMA composites produced by in situ polymerization and solution mixing demonstrated a 60.7% and 20% improvement in tensile strength, respectively [ 82 ,  83 ]. The GBC has shown promise in a variety of materials worldwide that require high mechanical strength, low weight, and high flexibility [ 78 ,  84 ].

sections.heading: Thermal Properties
paragraphs: Since non-doped graphene has a low density, phonon transport governs thermal conductivity rather than electronic conductivity, as shown in Fig.  3  (b) [ 85 ]. Theoretical and experimental investigations confirmed that graphene has 3000–5300 W/m K thermal conductivity. While comparable to carbon nanotubes, this value was much higher than that of diamonds and graphite. Effective heat conduction may be shown by gate vibration or phononic models through the sp 2  hybridization of strong C-C bonds [ 86 ].

Theoretically, a composite with better thermal properties can be made by mixing a small amount of graphene with polymers [ 78 ,  84 ]. Numerous studies have examined the thermal stability and conductivity of graphene oxide-based materials, including 25% rGO-Epoxy, 0.3% rGO-Epoxy by weight, 2% rGO-PS, 0.7% GO-PVA, and 3% rGO-PLA [ 87 ,  88 ,  89 ,  90 – 91 ]. A 25 vol% rGO filler in epoxy may increase the heat conductivity by almost 3000%. According to a study, the composites synthesized by Yu et al. outperformed traditional carbon material fillers in terms of thermal conductivity, with a value of k = 6.44 W/m K. The composite’s heat conductivity may be limited, nevertheless, due to the filler-matrix contact. Graphene oxide was functionalized by Hu et al. to enhance the composite’s interfacial adhesion and solve this problem [ 92 ]. Adding 0.5 vol% graphene oxide to the epoxy increased its thermal conductivity by 800%. The composite outperformed carbon nanotube (CNT) infused composites in terms of heat conductivity by 30%. In contrast to CNTs, which have a one-dimensional structure, Bui et al. showed that graphene oxide-based materials (GBC) exhibit higher thermal conductivity than graphene’s two-dimensional structure [ 93 ].

Adding graphene or a derivative to a polymer matrix composite may increase the composite’s thermal stability and flame retardancy. This takes into account graphene’s exceptional thermal stability as a barrier that prevents combustion gas transfer. Compared with a polymer matrix without graphene, GBC with a small amount of graphene added might exhibit much better thermal stability [ 79 ]. Guo et al. combined epoxy with reduced graphene oxide (rGO) to form a composite, which was investigated for its combustibility [ 88 ]. At 5 wt% rGO, the results showed a 43.9% drop in the total heat release rate. According to a study, GBC can be used in heat applications, including as electronic components, due to its conductivity and stability [ 79 ].

sections.heading: Impermeability
paragraphs: Because of its (i) high electron density, (ii) densely packed carbon atoms, (iii) firmly overlapped sheets, and (iv) high resistance, graphene is impenetrable to several gases and compounds. One of the most impermeable materials known to science is graphene. There were claims made in 2008 regarding potential new uses for graphene-based materials’ impermeability, including selective gas permeation, preservation of water molecule layers, confinement in wet electron microscopy, nanoporous bio-scale structures, and ultra-thin composite corrosion coatings. For permeability, the selected synthesis technique is critical as it influences flaws [ 94 ]. Adding graphene to PVA significantly increased its water impermeability, as reported by Wang et al. [ 95 ]. Composites made with 1wt% rGO had a water absorption ratio of 48.8%, down from 105.2% for pure PVA. Not only that, GBC has excellent barrier capabilities, such as being impermeable to gases like O 2 , N 2 , and He [ 96 ,  97 – 98 ]. Biological devices and packaging materials rely heavily on gas and water barrier properties [ 78 ,  99 ].

sections.heading: Electrical Conductivity
paragraphs: More people are interested in graphene’s electrical characteristics than in its other amazing features. Graphene has a distinct configuration of Fermi energy levels and a linear Dirac-like spectrum, suggesting that it may be an inherent semiconductor as shown in Fig.  3  (c) [ 100 ]. The parabolic spectrum of double-layer graphene is very tiny and insignificant, with a band overlap of 1.6 meV. So, it may be thought of as a metal with a special form of exciton. An excess of three layers of graphene belt should be shown by many load carriers across the valence and conduction bands [ 101 ,  102 ].

Adding graphene to polymers to enhance their electrical characteristics has been the subject of many studies. 1 vol% rGO-HDPE, 2 wt% rGO-PU, 3–5 wt% rGO-PLA, and 1 vol% rGO-PS were among the tested graphene oxide-based composites (GBC) [ 103 ,  104 ,  105 – 106 ]. A GBC with as little as 1 vol% rGO reportedly exhibits electrical conductivity ten times higher than pure polystyrene (PS) [ 106 ].

An ideal electrically conductive GBC has a filler network that is both effective and conductive [ 78 ]. This ensures improved conductivity with less graphene filler, which is the lower limit for the insulator to conductor transition. The lower limit for the volume of graphene in the GBC affects the economic feasibility for maintaining the processability of the composite and the cost of the components. The electrical properties of graphene/polymer composites are influenced by the aspect ratio, dispersion state, contact resistance, the quality of the connected 3D network, and intrinsic electrical conductivity. Furthermore, GBC shows improved electrical conductivity over CNT-based composites. Due to graphene’s properties, including (i) an increased surface area impediting agglomeration, (ii) a lower aspect ratio from wrinkling and crimping, and (iii) a 2D planar structure resulting in multiple contact points, GBC can be used in a variety of applications that require electrical conductivity [ 78 ].

sections.heading: Biological Characteristics
paragraphs: The majority of graphene oxide and its derivatives have demonstrated cytocompatibility both in vitro and in vivo, as shown in Fig.  3  (d). On the other hand, 2D materials may affect cellular function due to their physicochemical characteristics. There are two aspects to the functioning of graphene surfaces: surface concentration and aggregation states. When transported across cell membranes, graphene’s rough edges might damage cells. Its aggregated form has the potential to cause cell death in some cases. Due to decreased steric hindrance, nanoscale graphene is related to cytotoxicity, inflammation, and genotoxicity, all of which are undesirable results. In addition, cells quickly absorb functionalized graphene (GO, FGO, and rGO), particularly at nanoscale levels, which causes greater breakdown of cell membranes. There are tissue engineering uses for graphene oxide and its derivatives, which also have antibacterial characteristics. A great deal of research has focused on the processes that allow graphene oxide to exert its antibacterial properties, such as photo-thermal effects, basal plane, oxidative stress, entrapment, and membrane tension [ 107 ]. The sharp edges of GO have the potential to damage cell membranes, which might trigger the membrane stress response system. For some bacteria, such as  Pseudomonas aeruginosa  and  Staphylococcus aureus , the GO structure enables electron abstraction at the cell membrane, weakening the cell wall and ultimately killing the organism. In particular,  E. coli  and other bacteria are susceptible to oxidative stress and ultimate death when exposed to GO and rGO because of the functionalized groups on their surfaces, which may change the intracellular partial pressure of oxygen. Photothermal therapy uses graphene oxide to enhance antibacterial activity, as the two substances exhibit synergistic effects when combined with laser light. An important reason why GO-based materials have antioxidant action is that they need sp 2  carbons for electron transfer and radical adduct formation [ 108 ,  109 ]. Because of this quality, these biomaterials have the potential to protect cells from oxidative stress by effectively neutralizing free radicals. Toxic effects, immune system reactions, and environmental risks are major concerns with non-biodegradable graphene (not including FGO). In an oxygen-rich environment, GO can be oxidized by horseradish peroxidase and hydrogen peroxide. Biomaterials, like scaffolds, need to degrade at the same rate as tissues and organs; hence, there have been several attempts to speed up the biodegradation of GBCs [ 110 ]. Functional groups on the surface of GO significantly increase the bioactivity of polymers, as shown by Wan and Chen [ 111 ]. This led researchers to conclude that GO’s beneficial bioactivity was responsible for the calcium phosphate buildup on the GBC surface. Graphene oxide-based materials have been developed as viable alternatives for biomedical applications owing to their superior biocompatibility and the ability to be functionalized with biomolecules, thereby enhancing their specificity and efficacy. Their effective incorporation into drug delivery systems facilitates the regulated and prompt release of therapeutic agents, tackling issues associated with medication stability, bioavailability, and targeted delivery [ 112 ].

sections.heading: Biocompatibility and Toxicity
paragraphs: Biocompatibility remains a critical determinant for the clinical translation of graphene oxide (GO)-based nanomaterials. While GO offers exceptional surface chemistry and dispersibility, its toxicity profile is highly context-dependent, influenced by physicochemical parameters (lateral size, oxidation degree, surface functionalization), exposure route, and biological model. Recent systematic evaluations emphasize the need to distinguish in vitro cytotoxicity from in vivo outcomes and to address dose-dependency and regulatory hurdles [ 113 ].

In vitro findings consistently demonstrate dose-dependent cytotoxicity, primarily driven by oxidative stress, membrane disruption, and ROS generation. Pristine GO typically induces significant cell viability reduction above 50 µg mL⁻¹ in epithelial, macrophage, and cancer cell lines, whereas functionalized GO (PEGylated, protein-coated, or reduced forms) shows markedly improved cytocompatibility, with viability often exceeding 90% even at higher concentrations [ 114 ]. In vivo studies, however, reveal a more nuanced picture. In rodent models, high-dose GO administration can trigger acute pulmonary inflammation, fibrosis, and organ accumulation in a clear dose- and time-dependent manner. In contrast, recent large-animal data are far more reassuring: a 2025 pilot study in swine demonstrated that water-dispersible pristine graphene and GO elicited only modest local tissue reactions following intraperitoneal injection, with no evidence of systemic toxicity or significant immunological activation [ 113 ].

Most notably, the first-in-human controlled inhalation trial exposed healthy volunteers to thin, highly purified GO nanosheets for two hours under double-blind conditions; no adverse effects on pulmonary function, cardiovascular parameters, or systemic inflammation markers were observed, establishing acute tolerability in humans for the first time [ 115 ]. Dose-dependency emerges as the dominant factor across both in vitro and in vivo settings: low-to-moderate doses (< 10–50 µg mL⁻¹ or equivalent in vivo) are generally well-tolerated or even bioactive (e.g., promoting cell adhesion), while higher exposures consistently exacerbate ROS-mediated damage, genotoxicity, and chronic inflammation. Surface modification and controlled lateral size (< 1 μm) further reduce these risks by enhancing biodegradability via neutrophil myeloperoxidase and enzymatic pathways [ 113 ]. Regulatory concerns centre on the absence of standardized testing protocols, batch-to-batch variability, long-term biodistribution/clearance data, and scalability under Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP). Agencies such as the FDA and EMA require harmonized nano-specific guidelines for nanomedicines, including chronic toxicity, immunogenic potential, and environmental impact assessments—areas where GO currently lacks comprehensive datasets [ 115 ].

sections.heading: Biocompatibility of Graphene Oxide-Based Materials
paragraphs: Graphene oxide has emerged as a very adaptable nanomaterial for biomedical applications due to its extensive specific surface area, many oxygen-containing functional groups, superior dispersibility in aqueous environments, and straightforward surface functionalization [ 116 ]. It is essential to evaluate the biocompatibility, toxicological effects, and potential environmental impacts of graphene and its byproducts before integrating it into human tissue, particularly for implant applications. Much excitement surrounds graphene oxide-based sensors and their potential uses in biotechnology and health monitoring. There have been a lot of studies done on graphene oxide-based nanomaterials [ 117 ]. To this day, there has been no comprehensive analysis of the effects on ecosystems and human health. For new materials, thorough safety evaluations are necessary. Biosensors are analytical tools that combine biophysical detectors with functional chemicals or biological components to detect biological analytes. This device can convert your biological data into a more measurable signal. The durability, environmental sensitivity, and remarkable biological compatibility of graphene oxide make it an ideal material for real-time sensing devices and point-of-care applications [ 118 ]. Chemical sensing is one of the fastest-growing industries, and new materials are crucial for its success. Graphene oxide meets all the requirements to produce efficient sensors because of its extraordinary characteristics. It is quite challenging to implement new sensory systems that can replace its unique properties. The electrical and optical properties of a single living molecule or biomolecule on or near the graphene oxide surface may be altered by charge or energy transfer produced by localized deformation [ 119 ]. Graphene Oxide contains several oxygen-containing functional groups (including hydroxyl, epoxide, and carbonyl) predominantly at the edges and surfaces, significantly influencing sensor performance via chemical interactions, adsorption, and charge transfer. The ripples, residual functional groups, layers, and sheet dimensions significantly affect the sensitivity and selectivity of GO-based sensors [ 120 ,  121 ]. Research indicates that surface properties, including atomic-level bonding configuration and nanoscale morphology, markedly affect the biological activity of graphene oxide-based materials by improving hemocompatibility, cellular adhesion, and proliferation, underscoring the significance of surface engineering in the development of clinically relevant biomaterials [ 122 ].

Graphene oxide (GO)-based nanomaterials remain largely preclinical, with limited progression to human studies. The landmark first-in-human trial involved 14 healthy volunteers who inhaled thin, ultra-pure GO nanosheets (200 µg m⁻³) for two hours under double-blind, controlled conditions. No adverse effects were observed on lung function, blood pressure, heart rate, or systemic inflammation markers, demonstrating acute tolerability of carefully designed GO (ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT03659864) [ 123 ].

In the field of neurosurgery, interim findings of the first-in-human clinical trial (NCT06368310) using graphene-based cortical electrodes for brain tumor resection surgery, conducted by INBRAIN Neuroelectronics, have been published. Neuroelectronic (2025) published findings from the first four patients that resolved the hypothesis about device-associated negative events. Additionally, the findings demonstrated excellent signal resolution, including the resolution of high-frequency gamma activity, and the intraoperative performance of the electrodes was excellent and safe [ 124 ]. In spite of excellent safety findings, there have been no Phase I/II clinical trials of any GO-based therapeutic products (i.e. drugs, imaging, or scaffolds). Significant barriers still exist in the arena of regulatory affairs. Both the FDA and EMA have no specific approval pathway for graphene. Currently, they review the materials in situ and evaluate extended restrictions by considering general nanomaterial guidelines. These include long-term studies of dissemination in the human body, immunological response assessments, and compliance with conditions of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) [ 125 ,  126 ].

sections.heading: Biological Sensing
paragraphs: Graphene oxide is extensively utilized in biological sensing applications owing to its remarkable characteristics, such as a high surface area, biocompatibility, and the presence of oxygen-containing functional groups that promote strong interactions with biomolecules [ 127 ]. GO effectively extinguishes fluorescence through energy transfer, facilitating the sensitive detection of DNA, RNA, proteins, and tiny molecules by observing fluorescence variations. It also serves as a matrix to enhance the ionization of biomolecules for sensitive mass spectrometry-based identification of diverse bioanalytes [ 128 ]. The hydrophilicity and biocompatibility of GO facilitate robust, precise interactions with nucleic acids, proteins, and other biomolecules. The adjustable surface chemistry enables the development of hybrid nanocomposites designed for various biosensing platforms. These attributes of GO provide ultrasensitive, real-time detection appropriate for medical diagnostics, environmental surveillance, and food safety [ 129 ]. Hasler et al. developed clickable graphene nanoribbons for use in electrochemical sensors that detect interleukin 6 by using nanoribbons as interface linkers for rGO-based field-effect transistor sensors [ 130 ].

sections.heading: Graphene Oxide-Based Materials for Sensing Biomolecules
DNA Sensing
paragraphs: This innovative detection device, which uses water-soluble graphene oxide as a structure for precise DNA identification, is simplified in the following diagram. GO can fully obstruct the fluorescence of dye-labeled sDNA by binding to it, given that GO has been demonstrated to exhibit strong noncovalent interactions with nucleobases and aromatic compounds. The binding of dye-labeled DNA changes the shape of the target molecule, which disturbs the interaction between GO and the dye-labeled DNA when a target is present. When the dye-labeled DNA is released from the GO via interactions, its fluorescence is restored. Because of its sensitivity and specificity towards the targeted molecule, this approach has the potential to deliver fluorescence-enhanced sensing. Graphene oxide found in this research is a good platform for sensitive, targeted biomolecule detection, just like carbon nanotubes. However, GO is a better material for biosensor development than CNTs because it is cheaper and can be produced at an enormous scale [ 131 ,  132 ]. Liu et al. designed a fluorescent aptamer sensor utilizing graphene oxide (GO) for the detection of thrombin. Fluorescein-labeled thrombin aptamer was formed in Tris-HCl buffer and combined with thrombin for 5 min at ambient temperature. The hybridization process lasted approximately 30 min, resulting in fluorescence recovery due to the aptamer-thrombin interaction. The fluorescence was observable within a spectrum of 1 nm to 1 mm. The sensor provided a sensitive, specific FRET-based approach for thrombin detection, exhibiting significant signal changes upon interaction [ 133 ].

sections.heading: Protein Sensing
paragraphs: Graphene oxide (GO) is considered a significant material for protein sensing because of its extensive surface area, superior water dispersibility, and extensive oxygen-containing functional groups that promote conjugation with biomolecules [ 134 ]. Its excellent fluorescence quenching potential and facilitation of electron transfer make it optimal for developing sensitive and selective biosensing systems [ 135 ]. GO interacts with target proteins primarily through hydrogen bonding, electrostatic interactions, and π–π stacking, facilitating detection via several techniques, including electrochemical methods, fluorescence resonance energy transfer (FRET), and Raman spectroscopy [ 136 ,  137 ].

A new photoluminescence test for measuring protein kinase activity has been developed by researchers. It uses graphene quantum dots and is both fast and accurate. Using a new approach that depends on the targeted buildup of phosphorylated peptide-GQDs caused by the coordination of Zr 4+  ions, a kinase-catalyzed phosphorylation of peptides was observed. In contrast to the conventional FRET quenching procedures employed in enzyme tests that rely on fluorescence, this approach offers a novel and attractive alternative. Prompt detection (within 5 min) and an easy investigation procedure that avoids complex protein identification processes are only two of the many benefits of this technology, which uses peptide-conjugated GQDs, over existing fluorescent kinase approaches. Development of kinase-related drugs and assessment of kinase inhibitors are two areas that might benefit from the suggested approach. Pan et al. designed a paper-based SERS biosensor (enPSERS) utilizing graphene oxide–gold nanostar (GO-GNS) hybrids for the sensitive, label-free detection of free bilirubin in blood serum. The GO-GNS exhibited elevated SERS sensitivity, bilirubin enrichment, and fluorescence quenching, with adsorption governed by electrostatic and π–π interactions, as described by a pseudo-second-order kinetic model. The biosensor attained two linear detection ranges (5.0–150 µM and 150–500 µM) with a minimal detection limit of 0.436 µM and showed high concordance with the commercial diazo technique, indicating its potential for precise clinical diagnosis of jaundice. Figure  4  (a) illustrates the fabrication of the enPSERS biosensor, wherein GO–GNS hybrids (121% GNS: GO) were applied on filter paper, resulting in a dark blue hue attributed to the hybrid coating. Figure  4  (b) shows the SERS mapping results utilizing 4-NTP, exhibiting consistent Raman signals across an extensive area with minimal fluctuation (RSD ~ 5%), and Fig.  4  (c) presents the optical image and the associated SERS image of the enPSERS biosensor utilizing 4-NTP as a probe molecule. The SERS mapping of the N–O band at 1328 cm − 1  over a 1200 μm × 1000 μm area demonstrated a consistent signal distribution. The minimal relative standard deviation (RSD = 0.05) validates the uniform distribution of gold nanostars on graphene oxide nanosheets, guaranteeing consistent hot spot formation and illustrating the high quality and reproducibility of the biosensor [ 138 ]. Graphene and gold were used to build a biosensor that relies on surface plasmon resonance [ 139 ]. A single- or triple-step grating design was chosen due to the fact that the refractive indices of water, glucose, and blood are all different, so that it could detect them more accurately.

sections.heading: Bio-Electrochemical Sensors
paragraphs: The big pores improve binding partner detection by allowing the analyte to move more freely. Direct detection systems based on graphene have the potential to discover important biological components even at low concentrations. New electrochemical sensors are showing interest in graphene oxide due to its unique morphological and electrochemical properties. Due to the rapid electron transit rate at graphene’s edges and defects, rGO layers or small pieces of pure graphene are well-suited for use in electrochemical experiments [ 140 ]. The inherent catalytic activity of reduced graphene oxide makes it useful for sensor-based enzymatic applications; it produces many minor enzymatic products, including hydrogen peroxide and NADH. Electrodes that are grounded in graphene have a huge operational reaction area and can pack enzymatically because of their extraordinarily high surface-area-to-volume ratio (theoretically 2600 m 2 g − 1 ). The excellent strength-to-weight ratio and potential for percolating charge conduction channels created by even a little quantity of graphene make it a promising candidate for use in functional composites. Reduced graphene oxide is the preferred material for the majority of graphene sensors due to several reasons, such as rGO’s excellent electrochemical performance, which is guaranteed by its abundance of defects and functional groups, surface chemical moieties make it versatile and adaptable for various applications, which improve sensor efficacy, electrical and chemical properties are highly adjustable, and rGO shows effective electrical conductivity, unlike nonconductive GO.

sections.heading: Bioimaging
paragraphs: Academic and clinical contexts both rely heavily on bioimaging, particularly when trying to understand the inner workings of cells, tissues, and organs, as well as abnormal disease processes. Due to insufficient sensitivity, specificity, and targeting, bioimaging methods have limited medical use. Therefore, it is crucial to develop a range of imaging techniques that are suitable for certain uses. Photography, fluorescence MRI, photoacoustic imaging, and Raman spectroscopy imaging are the four primary imaging modalities that make use of GBNs  ( Table  1 ) .

sections.heading: Fluorescence Imaging
paragraphs: In fluorescence imaging (FRI) applications, graphene oxide-based materials play a vital role due to their surface and edge defects, suitable band gaps, and outstanding light stability, which give them strong fluorescence characteristics. GO-based materials have limited use in vivo FRI because of their low fluorescence quantum yield. The use of fluorescent dyes for the covalent or noncovalent functionalization of GO is essential to overcome this limitation and enhance FRI signals. GO can serve as a carrier for various photosensitizers in FRI studies [ 152 ]. It is possible to monitor the distribution and delivery of medications in vivo in real-time via intramolecular charge transfer, which may substantially improve fluorescence performance. Hydrophilic lanthanum nanocrystals were synthesized and exhibit robust visible/NIR-II luminescence. Encapsulating them in GO allowed them to accomplish intracellular tracking, microRNA-21 detection, and tumor targeting NIR-II imaging in vivo. Additionally, they showed a strong response around 1525 nm.

Song et al. reported an intelligently assembled biosensor based on catalytic hairpin assembly (CHA) and aggregation-induced emission (AIE), referred to as catalytic hairpin aggregation-induced emission (CHAIE), for the ultrasensitive detection and intracellular imaging of miRNA-155. Both the detection sensitivity of miRNA liquid biopsy and intracellular imaging are hindered by the low abundance, diverse expression, and temporal variations of miRNAs across distinct cellular sites. These issues were overcome by them. To do this, graphene oxide was used to quench the fluorescence, and tetraphenylethylene-N3 was utilized as the AIE luminogen. Because the CHA reaction was initiated when the target miRNA was present, the AIEgen was able to self-assemble with the hairpin DNA. A robust AIE fluorescence signal was created, and the intramolecular rotation of the AIEgen was limited by this arrangement. The CHAIE biosensor was notable for its quick detection since it did not need enzymes or costly heat cycling equipment. The biosensor detected miRNA at concentrations ranging from 2 pM to 200 nM in as little as 30 min under ideal conditions, with a limit of detection of 0.42 pM, as shown in Fig.  5  (a-d). Due to its great sensitivity and minimal background signal, the CHAIE biosensor is ideal for accurate spatiotemporal imaging of target miRNA in live cells [ 153 ].

sections.heading: Magnetic Resonance Imaging
paragraphs: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) has replaced other methods in bioimaging because of its noninvasiveness, high spatial resolution, and infinite tissue penetration depth. Manganese and gadolinium are the two most popular contrast agents utilized in MRI scans [ 157 ,  158 ]. However, in vivo, nonselective coordination results in substantial nonspecific toxicity. Chelating harmful paramagnetic metal ions is one way that graphene oxide-based materials with different functional groups lessen their toxicity. The oxygen-containing functional groups on graphene oxide, including carboxyl, hydroxyl, epoxy, and phenolic groups, offer active sites that can bind and stabilize paramagnetic ions such as Gd 3+ , Mn 2+ , and Fe 3 O 4  nanoparticles. This chelation reduces the release of free ions that commonly induce toxicity in biological systems [ 159 ].

Graphene-based magnetic nanocarriers exhibit exceptional performance and biocompatibility for MRI applications. GO-based materials integrated with magnetic nanoparticles, such as iron oxide nanoparticles (IONPs), enhance MRI signals by improving relaxivity and circulation stability. GO-IONP hybrids significantly enhance T2 relaxivity compared to nanoparticles alone, thereby facilitating superior cellular and in vivo imaging [ 160 ]. GO composites have been investigated for multifunctional theranostic applications that integrate MRI with medication delivery and photothermal therapy for cancer treatment [ 161 ]. Rodriguez et al. indicated that graphene oxide/iron oxide (Fe 3 O 4 ) nanocomposites acted as multifunctional MRI contrast agents with less toxicity owing to the chelation of GO of iron ions. The nanocomposites demonstrated augmented MRI signal and superior biocompatibility by inhibiting the release of free iron ions [ 144 ].

Su et al. reported a novel strategy for constructing graphene oxide nanomaterials with significantly enhanced photothermal (PT) and photoacoustic (PA) performance in the near-infrared (NIR) II biowindow through chemical reduction. Chemically reduced graphene oxide nanomaterials showed considerable improvement in optical absorption over the whole NIR spectrum, from NIR-I to NIR-II, based on their optical spectra. The improvement was attributed to the graphene oxide sheets reestablishing electronic conjugation, leading to the black-body reintroduction effect observed in most graphite-like materials. The recommended procedure was evaluated by synthesizing CR-G samples with varying degrees of reduction. The testing results revealed that the CR-G samples’ PT performance improved significantly because the chemical decrease increased the absorption of the NIR-II biowindow, as shown in Fig.  5  (e-h). In addition, CR-G samples with varied degrees of reduction were scanned utilizing PA both in vitro and in vivo, demonstrating better NIR-II PA capabilities. As a consequence of chemical reduction, graphene oxide nanoparticles have immense potential for PT and PA applications in the near-infrared (NIR-II) biowindow, and this study provides useful guidelines for their rational design [ 154 ].

sections.heading: Photoacoustic Imaging
paragraphs: Noninvasive photoacoustic imaging uses tissue or contrast agent absorption of electromagnetic waves of low-power, non-ionizing laser light. After that, it uses visual processing to gather sound waves, then uses focused heating to create broadband sound waves by converting light waves into sound. The biomedical community views photoacoustic imaging (PAI) as a highly promising imaging modality due to its ability to image deep tissues and organs with remarkable spatial resolution. More precisely localized blood vessels and melanomas may also be seen. Haemoglobin and melanin are examples of endogenous contrast agents (CA) that have a major impact on the results of imaging. Accordingly, CAs play a pivotal role in achieving optimal imaging performance in PAI [ 162 ]. Not long ago, diffusion of GO-based nanomaterials in PAI showed remarkable near-infrared absorption. When it comes to deep organs and tissues, GO-based nanomaterials have better spatial resolution than pure FRI. Possible improvements to contrast and speckle are also in the works. Due to its larger sp 2  domains, rGO exhibits improved absorption of near-infrared light, making it an ideal photoacoustic contrast agent. For photoacoustic imaging and photothermal treatment of pancreatic cancer, the study synthesized a reduced graphene oxide@gold nanostar. Following surface cross-linking on the rGO@AuNS, folic acid binds specifically to tumor cell folate receptors. The imaging performance of receptor-mediated endocytosis and targeting effectiveness are both greatly enhanced by this. The ability of rGO to absorb near-infrared light is connected to the synthetic system’s effectiveness. Regarding the photoacoustic signal, rGO@AuNS outperforms both bare gold nanostars and unreduced graphene oxide. On the other hand, rGO is less hydrophilic than GO, which might lead to worse biocompatibility. A one-step reduction of bovine serum albumin is one possible step in the production of rGO. This leads to rGO with good monodispersion, small size (approximately 70 nm), little cytotoxicity, and exceptional stability. The peak of the rGO PAI signal in cancer in in vivo experiments was at 30 min, and it stayed there for at least four hours [ 163 ].

Additionally, the initial graphene might serve as a PAI agent by modifying polymers like PVA or PEG [ 163 ,  164 ]. Graphene can become an ultrasensitive contrast agent due to its notable absorption in the near-infrared (NIR) region when it forms a complex with indocyanine green via π-π stacking interactions [ 165 ,  166 ].

Einafshar et al. presented a novel approach to treating prostate cancer using a nanocarrier composed of folic acid (FA), β-cyclodextrin (β-CD), and magnetic graphene oxide (MGO) as a theranostic agent, as shown in Fig.  5  (i). Curcumin is a potential therapy for prostate cancer, and the carrier was designed to improve its bioavailability and solubility. The overexpression of folic acid receptors on solid tumor surfaces, such as prostate cancer, implies that these receptors might be exploited to direct medicine delivery to tumor cells, lowering the risk of nonspecific adverse effects on healthy tissues. The Folic acid-curcumin@β-CD-MGO nanocarrier was tested in vitro against LNCaP (androgen-dependent) and PC3 (androgen-independent) prostate cancer cells to assess its anticancer efficiency. Cell growth was suppressed, oxidative damage was generated, and apoptotic effects were boosted, with the effects being concentration dependent. Nanoparticle relaxometry indicated that the material might be employed as an MRI negative contrast agent [ 155 ]. Overall, this work reveals a promising theranostic agent that increases curcumin distribution, allows for traceability, and promotes its therapeutic potential in the treatment of prostate cancer.

sections.heading: Raman Spectroscopy Imaging
paragraphs: Raman spectroscopy relies on molecular vibrational excitation and inelastic scattering of phonons from the sample. RSI is a potent analytical technique that enhances the capabilities of vibrational spectroscopy. It has a good signal-to-noise ratio, little photobleaching, and the ability to multiplex without invasive or harmful procedures. The field of biomedicine makes frequent use of it, particularly in bioimaging. The inherent Raman emissions of GO-based nanomaterials are unique, and it is possible to increase imaging sensitivity by improving Surface-Enhanced Raman Spectroscopy (SERS) by coating GO-based nanomaterials with metal nanoparticles like gold or silver. This property has attracted considerable attention from researchers seeking to use GO as imaging probes in biological cells. Graphene oxide’s in situ reduction of silver ions improved the surface-enhanced Raman scattering of the silver/GO hybrid, which led to brighter and more discernible Raman imaging signals than the original GO. This finding is very noteworthy. The use of folic acid in conjunction with Ag/GO nanoparticles allowed for targeted SERS imaging of cancer cells by targeting the folate receptor [ 167 ].
GBNs find use in radionuclide imaging, multimodal imaging, and computed tomography imagery.

Zarei et al. explored the surface functionalization of magnesium (Mg)-based alloys with diopside-graphene oxide coatings to improve the biocompatibility and corrosion resistance of these biodegradable materials for bone tissue engineering. Coatings of varying concentrations of graphene oxide (x = 0, 0.03, 0.06, and 0.12 g/L) were applied to AZ31 alloy via electrophoretic deposition. Surface features, corrosion resistance, bioactivity, antibacterial capabilities, and cytocompatibility of the coated and untreated substrates were the primary outcomes of this investigation. Powdered diopside was produced by means of the sol-gel technique. Among the coatings tested, the Dio/0.06GO nanocomposite exhibited the most compact morphology, as observed by Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy. The surface roughness of the Dio/0.12GO sample increased as the GO content increased, according to Atomic Force Microscopy experiments, which also revealed a Sa value of 293.80 ± 23.75 nm as shown in Fig.  5  (j). The wettability of the coatings followed a similar pattern. With a corrosion current density (icorr) 91.5% lower than that of the uncoated Mg alloy, the Dio/0.06GO coating showed the best corrosion resistance. On top of that, after 7 days of submersion in SBF, this coating had the highest Ca/P atomic ratio (1.61), indicating it was the most bioactive of the bunch. The antibacterial activity test revealed that GO had a bactericidal impact on  E. coli  and  S. aureus , especially at higher doses. Although the Dio/0.12GO coating showed the best MCT3T-E1 osteoblast cellular attachment in vitro cellular assays, the Dio/0.06GO coatings had the greatest cell viability at 92.17 ± 1.2%. It can be concluded that Dio/GO nanocomposite coatings have the ability to enhance the biological characteristics and corrosion resistance of Mg alloy orthopedic applications [ 156 ].

sections.heading: Drug Delivery
paragraphs: A number of biomedical research projects have looked at the potential of GO for drug delivery in recent years. There has been a lot of research into the biological applications of GO-based materials, particularly in smart medication delivery. Strategies for the non-covalent incorporation of medicinal compounds into materials based on graphene include stacking interactions, hydrophobic interactions, and hydrogen bonding [ 181 ]. To transport cancer medications that are insoluble in water, Liu et al. suggested using a combination of GO, PEG, and SN38, which shows that the former is soluble in water and that the latter is effective when dissolved in organic solvents. By using the MTS test, NGO-PEG-SN38 was able to effectively eradicate the human colon cancer cell line HCT-116 in vitro. With a half-growth-inhibition concentration of around 10 µM, the water-soluble medication CPT-11 has reduced toxicity [ 182 ].

Nanohybrids made of non-genetically-modified organisms and hematin-terminated dextran were used to eradicate drug-resistant MCF-7/ADR cells [ 183 ]. Under physiological conditions, NGO-HDex showed better stability than pure NGO. Furthermore, an efficient combination of NGO-HDex with the anticancer drug DOX, with a loading capacity of 3.4 mg mg − 1 , is possible [ 184 ]. Dinda et al. have shown the potential of DOX and ZnS: Mn-doped nanocrystals attached to GO for cellular labeling and drug administration. The maximal DOX trapping efficacy was 100% when 1000 g mL − 1  of GO-PEG/ZnS: Mn composite particles were incubated with a 100 g mL − 1  DOX solution [ 185 ]. Cell death of around 85% occurs in HeLa cancer cells when exposed to the drug-laden DOX nanocomposite at a concentration of 10 g mL − 1 , in contrast to cells loaded with free DOX, which show cell death of approximately 68%.

Chen et al. created a medication delivery method where a saturation loading capacity of 65% was achieved at a DOX content of 0.3 mg mL − 1  in the mixed solution. Using PEG-fGO to create Fe 3 O 4  nanoparticles. The hybrid shows an enhanced binding ability, attaining a loading capacity of 0.27 mg mg − 1 , at a 5-fluorouracil concentration of 0.5 mg mL − 1  [ 186 ]. The hybrid shows an enhanced binding ability, attaining a loading capacity of 0.27 mg mg − 1 , at a 5-fluorouracil concentration of 0.5 mg mL − 1 . The use of graphene-based magnetic and plasmonic nanocomposites demonstrated the facilitation of medication distribution using magnetic field.

In summary, up to 90% drug loading capacity and responsive drug release make functionalized GO/rGO platforms even more effective than conventional drug carriers. A main challenge is the reproducibility of the GO/rGO platforms in different batches. Potential toxicity and slow clinical translation are also important challenges. To improve the translation of this technology into the clinic, the focus should be on scalable Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) production and multi-centric preclinical studies.

sections.heading: Gene Delivery
paragraphs: Gene transfer is a good fit for graphene oxide-based materials because of its great transfection capabilities and high loading efficiency. The process of gene delivery involves transferring foreign nucleic acids into eukaryotic cells. The specific method utilized to do this depends on the kind of cell and the goals of the experiment [ 187 ,  188 ]. The recipient cells may express the donated nucleic acid temporarily without reproducing it, or it might be permanently integrated into their genome and replicate with the host genome. Both outcomes can occur during gene delivery. Several techniques are often used to achieve transfection, including electroporation, lipofection, viral vectors, and ballistic particle delivery. The ability to alter the DNA of host cells has far-reaching implications for studying common biological processes, identifying disease molecular origins, and evaluating gene therapy efficacy. In recent years, transfection has gained significant attention due to its widespread usage in studying disease cellular processes and molecular pathways [ 189 ]. Recent advances in the field of life sciences have made it feasible to transfect human cells with a variety of nucleic acids. The short non-coding RNAs (siRNA, shRNA, and miRNA) are among them, along with DNA and RNA. Recombinant antibodies, proteins, and viral vectors have been generated by transfection techniques; they have found use in gene therapy, vaccines, and medicines. One must have a solid grasp of the distinction between transient transfection and continual transfection. Through the process of stable transfection, foreign DNA is integrated into the host nuclear genome, enabling the transgene to be produced forever [ 190 ,  191 ]. One may quantitatively assess the transfection effectiveness using real-time polymerase chain reaction, which evaluates the expression levels of certain foreign nucleic acids in a cell as well as other intracellular nucleic acids that may be affected by exogenous nucleic acids, such as microRNAs [ 192 ]. Efficient and viable transfection is a standard measure of transfection performance; improved transfection outcomes are linked to these factors. Transfection success is dependent on a myriad of factors, including DNA amount and quality, cell type, cell health, and transfection method. The transfection efficacy is highly dependent on the cell type and its pre-transfection physiological condition. The cells must be in good condition, able to grow, and free of any contaminants.

Sontakke et al. presented a novel approach to chemotherapy by utilizing targeted drug delivery systems for improved cancer treatment. Traditional chemotherapy is limited by its inability to selectively target cancer cells, leading to significant side effects. The study focused on overcoming these challenges through the development of self-assembled, sustainable, and straightforward nanocarriers for the delivery of caffeic acid, a natural chemotherapeutic agent. The β-CD-GO@MIL-100(Fe), also denoted as BGw-MF functionalized Fe-based metal-organic frameworks, were used in the synthesis of the nanocarriers, which did not include the use of hydrofluoric acid. The BGw-MF nanocarriers were characterized using a variety of techniques to look at their structural, functional, and morphological properties. The BGw-MF nanocarriers’ CA loading efficiency was measured, which changed with changes in the medium’s pH and the CA-to-nanocarrier ratio. The results demonstrated that BG0.5-MF had the highest loading efficiency, reaching 56.44 ± 2.25% at a 2 w/w ratio of CA in an alkaline environment (pH 9). Figure  6  (a-d) shows that the BG0.5-MF nanocarrier regulated the release pattern of CA, with a release of about 57.07 ± 2.01% at pH 5 and 48.04 ± 1.44% at pH 7.4. This controlled release pattern is advantageous for increasing drug release at tumor locations. Based on the results, BGw-MF nanocarriers might be a great CA-based anticancer DDS. Featuring a regulated release mechanism and a high medication loading capacity, the BG0.5-MF nanocarriers are promising for efficient and sustainable chemotherapy. The cytotoxicity results further highlight the suitability of BG0.5-MF for selective cancer treatment, offering a promising approach for future anticancer DDS [ 193 ].

Graphene oxide (GO)-based nanomaterials have emerged as superior non-viral vectors for gene delivery. Their ultrahigh surface area and oxygen functional groups enable high-capacity loading of nucleic acids (DNA, siRNA, mRNA) via π–π stacking and electrostatic interactions, while providing nuclease protection and stimuli-responsive release [ 194 ]. Functionalized GO-PEI hybrids demonstrate enhanced transfection efficiency and substantially reduced cytotoxicity compared to high-molecular-weight PEI. Unlike viral vectors plagued by immunogenicity and insertional mutagenesis risks, or liposomal carriers limited by stability and payload capacity, GO platforms offer greater biocompatibility, scalability, and multifunctionality for theranostic applications [ 195 ]. Recent studies on PEI-loaded GO quantum dots confirm superior uptake and gene expression in cancer cells with improved safety [ 194 ].

Overall, GO-based vectors excel in capacity and performance of both gene loading and gene delivery compared to traditional lipid or viral carriers. The cytotoxicity and inefficient endosomal escape along with the unwanted delivery of genes to other cells, pose challenges. The main effort should focus on biocompatibleGO surface designs validated through in vivo experiments.

sections.heading: Tissue Engineering
paragraphs: Repairing injured tissues and organs is the goal of tissue engineering, which entails creating artificial versions of these structures. As biomaterials advanced, they adapted to incorporate scaffolds, cells, and physiologically active substances into living tissues. Graphene oxide and its derivatives are a new class of materials that have the potential to revolutionize tissue engineering and healthcare applications. Shin et al. changed GO-GelMA hydrogels to improve cellular spreading, alignment, survival, and proliferation in a three-dimensional environment [ 196 ]. By combining the mechanical and electrical features of this GO reinforcement with a multi-stacking process, an easy way to create complex artificial tissues with cellular functioning and mechanical robustness may be achieved. Tissue engineering and regenerative medicine are both advanced by using GO as a protein-delivery vehicle within a 3D culture system for stem cell differentiation [ 197 ].

Making standing hydrogels of graphene oxide and hydroxyapatite is a simple process when it comes to making bone tissue [ 183 ]. One potential use of artificial hydrogels is the creation of artificial bone tissue, according to their remarkable characteristics [ 184 ]. Coating cracks and delamination were both reduced by using GO sheets in the sintered HA layer. Coatings made of GO and HA are more resistant to corrosion and have better adhesion strength than coatings made of pure HA [ 185 ]. Luong et al. assessed hydrogels containing graphene oxide (GO) and poly(ethylene glycol) methyl ether methacrylate (MEO2MA) for applications in wound healing. It was observed that GO-loaded hydrogels increased tensile strength (up to 626 kPa), appropriate elasticity, and significant swelling behavior, all of which are advantageous characteristics for skin tissue scaffolds. Biocompatibility was proven by non-toxic reactions in human dermal fibroblasts. In a rat wound healing model, the GO/MEO2MA hydrogels attained over 95% wound closure within 15 days, markedly surpassing the non-GO controls. Histological study revealed enhanced tissue regeneration, underscoring the therapeutic promise of GO-based wound dressings [ 198 ].

Li et al. synthesized graphene oxide/silk fibroin (GO/SF) scaffolds using a salt-leaching technique, followed by in situ reduction with ascorbic acid to produce rGO/SF scaffolds, aimed at replicating the porosity architecture of natural bone. SEM research demonstrated densely interconnected pores both at the surface and throughout the interior, with variable pore size depending on GO content. The FTIR spectra  ( Fig.  7  (a)) exhibited characteristic silk fibroin peaks at 1235, 1530, and 3280 cm⁻¹, thereby affirming the integrity of the silk fibroin structure, while the peak at 1410 cm⁻¹ indicated the presence of reduced graphene oxide (rGO). No new chemical bonds were established; however, examination of the amide I area  ( Fig.  7  (b)) demonstrated an increase in β-sheet content from 46.36% to 51.12%, signifying improved structural stability. Mechanical testing revealed that Young’s modulus rose from 5.5 ± 0.5 to 14.6 ± 2.1 kPa with increased rGO concentration. Biological assessment demonstrated enhanced MSC adherence, proliferation, and mineralisation in rGO/SF scaffolds relative to pure SF. Live/Dead staining  ( Fig.  7  (c)) demonstrated elevated cell viability, with increasing scaffold coverage by viable cells over a period of 8 weeks. The quantification of DNA content  ( Fig.  7  (d)) established a positive correlation between proliferation and rGO concentration, with the 3% rGO/SF scaffold facilitating the maximum cell density. The osteogenic differentiation markers BSP and RUNX2  ( Fig.  7  (e, f)) exhibited considerable upregulation in the presence of rGO, particularly in 1% and 3% scaffolds. After eight weeks, the 3% rGO/SF scaffolds demonstrated the highest expression of RUNX2. Calcium deposition study  ( Fig.  7  (g)) indicated that all scaffolds facilitated mineralisation throughout time, with the 3% rGO/SF scaffold exhibiting the highest calcium content after 8 weeks. The results showed that the integration of rGO improves β-sheet formation, mechanical stability, MSC proliferation, osteogenic gene expression, and mineral deposition, offering rGO/SF scaffolds viable options for bone tissue creation [ 199 ].

The considerable advances made in preclinical studies utilizing graphene oxide (GO) and reduced graphene oxide (rGO) makes their current technological challenges in shifting to the clinical practice of tissue engineering all the more disappointing. Limitations to scalability, as a result of batch to batch inconsistency in the degree of oxidation, lateral size, and functionalization of the graphene, impact the cost and compliance of Good Manufacturing Practice (GMP) production [ 200 ]. The absence of tailored pathways to graphene for the FDA and EMA means that researchers will be compelled to submit comprehensive and expensive studies to illuminate the challenges of chronic toxicity and other long-term safety concerns [ 200 ,  201 ]. The risks of long-term implantation include chronic infections, fibrosis, overstimulation of the antioxidant defense system, and incomplete biodegradation with the possibility of the material accumulating in various organs of the body, which justifies the need for extensive testing in large animal studies lasting more than six months with respect to the adoption of safety guidelines for clinical practice [ 202 ].

Therefore, low concentrations of rGO (1–3%) improve cell adhesion and osteogenesis causing differentiation in scaffolds. Responsive degradation and controlled 3D scaffold formation remain important challenges. The main focus of recent research should be aimed at developing intelligent and responsive GO scaffolds for personalised regenerative medicine and assessing their performance in vivo for extended periods.

sections.heading: Graphene Oxide-Based Materials in Theranostics
paragraphs: Theranostics is an advanced biomedical methodology that integrates diagnostic and therapeutic functions into a single platform, enabling concurrent disease identification, targeted intervention, and real-time assessment of therapeutic efficacy. In contrast to traditional methods, which divide diagnosis and therapy, theranostic systems offer a more efficient and individualized approach to disease management. Carbon nanomaterials, including quantum dots, graphene oxide, and graphene, have been extensively investigated for tumor detection, chemotherapy, photothermal therapy, photodynamic therapy, and associated biological uses [ 203 ]. Graphene can transport anticancer drugs into cancer cells within nanoparticles [ 204 ]. The surfaces of graphene have both covalent and noncovalent interactions, which are crucial for their interactions with cancer cells, tissues, and anticancer medications. A “smart” nanomaterial, graphene may activate its therapeutic characteristics by interacting with tumor microenvironments, pH levels, and endogenous and exogenous stimuli, according to many studies [ 205 ,  206 ].

Two important elements that impact the dynamics of tumor microenvironments are hydrogen peroxide and acidic pH. The effects of hydrogen peroxide may be imitated by a particular type of graphene oxide, N-GO, as shown by Lin et al. [ 207 ]. One of these things that happens with HeLa cancers is that the levels of reactive oxygen species rise, and the cancer cells die off because hydrogen peroxide is converted into ROS-hydroxyl radicals (HO). Normal cells and tissues are unaffected by HO radicals, despite their harmful nature. These steps might be useful because they lessen tumor medication resistance, lessen the likelihood of side effects in healthy cells and tissues, and make different tumor therapies more biocompatible.

Because their surface properties can be tuned to be either highly hydrophobic or highly hydrophilic, depending on the amount of graphene sheets and physical or chemical conjugation with different molecules such as surfactants and polyethylene glycol, graphene-based materials are attractive for gene and drug delivery. It is possible to adjust the distribution rate to meet individual needs by functionalizing the material in a way that produces an ideal hydrophilic-hydrophobic ratio. In addition, 2D graphene materials can absorb both visible and infrared light, which may lead to photothermia. This process is mostly used to trigger delivery [ 181 ].

Graphene is one of the nanocarriers used in gene therapy, a medical method that aims to treat or prevent disease by destroying harmful or genetically modified genes [ 208 ]. The potential eradication of colon cancer tumors in mouse models was found by Lo et al. to be facilitated by graphene quantum dots  ( Fig.  8 )  [ 209 ]. The GQDs were covalently attached to the cancer cells using polyethylenimine and green fluorescent proteins. After the tumor cell membrane was made permeable, doxorubicin was injected. Combining doxorubicin with the GQDs was more effective than using either drug alone in suppressing colon cancer tumors. When just the GQDs were present, the toxicity levels dropped.
