GO-based theranostic platforms have shown strong potential by combining imaging and therapy in a single system. Žárská et al. (2024) developed PEGylated GO nanoplatforms for dual-drug delivery (cisplatin derivative + doxorubicin) and achieved high loading capacity with controlled release, demonstrating significantly enhanced anticancer activity in 3D glioblastoma and osteosarcoma models compared to single-drug carriers [ 210 ]. Similarly, Wu et al. (2025) highlighted that functionalized GO improves tumour targeting and reduces multidrug resistance through synergistic chemo-photothermal effects [ 211 ].

However, critical comparison across studies reveals important limitations. While dual-drug GO systems offer superior therapeutic outcomes over monotherapy, they still face challenges such as burst release and complex synthesis. Pristine GO shows lower photothermal conversion efficiency and higher toxicity than PEGylated or mitochondria-targeted variants [ 125 ,  212 ]. Most studies remain at the in vitro or small-animal stage, with very limited long-term biodistribution and scalability data. Overall, functionalized GO platforms outperform unmodified GO in loading efficiency and efficacy, but none have yet progressed to clinical trials due to regulatory and reproducibility concerns.

To determine if the toxicity of the antineoplastic medication methotrexate is enhanced in tumors, GO has been used as a nanocarrier for the drug. Using pig skin fibroblasts, hepatocellular carcinoma cells, and human embryonic kidney cells, Abdelhamid and Hussein assessed the drug in combination with graphene [ 213 ]. Results showed that HEK293A cancer cells were more hazardous than normal cells. New evidence suggests that medications naturally lean toward nanocarriers. There are a lot of drugs that form hydrogen bonds and π-π interactions with the surface of graphene [ 214 ]. Graphene oxide (GO)-based nanomaterials have distinct advantages over traditional therapeutic systems by facilitating the integration of diagnostic and therapy within just one platform, hence providing targeted drug delivery, imaging guidance, and controlled release. Their extensive surface area, adjustable surface chemistry, and excellent water stability provide substantial drug loading and straightforward functionalization with targeting or imaging agents, enhancing precision and minimizing off-target toxicity. In theranostic applications, GO composites can provide photothermal or combined chemo-photothermal therapy, enhancing treatment efficacy compared to traditional single-function systems [ 215 ].

sections.heading: Infection Treatment Using Graphene-Based Materials
paragraphs: A thorough understanding of graphene’s processes and functions in biomedical applications requires an investigation into its antimicrobial and antibacterial characteristics. One common way to study microbial colonies is to observe their biofilm formation [ 216 ]. It is challenging to avoid microbial contamination of biofilms and other substances. The effectiveness of disease prevention and treatment is threatened by the rise of antibiotic resistance. To fight against antimicrobial (multi)resistant bacterial strains, it is crucial to find new antimicrobial medications. Materials connected to graphene might be included in such agents [ 217 ].

Ventilators, urinary catheters, and dental tools are just a few examples of the many medical devices that have been known to use various microbes. Reducing contamination levels requires the development of devices with antimicrobial coatings. Suitable nanomaterial layers or device coatings for germ elimination may be manufactured using 2D graphene oxide-based materials [ 218 ]. Studies on the microbiological activity of  E. coli  have made use of graphene and metal plates covered with GO. Graphene and GO aluminum plates had substantial antibacterial efficacy, and results showed that  E. coli  activity was suppressed. Graphene nanowalls have shown potent antibacterial properties against bacterial strains classified as Gram-positive and Gram-negative when applied as a coating on stainless steel substrates. The rough edges of the graphene nanowalls seemed to damage the bacterial membranes [ 219 ]. Yan et al. created a ternary rGO/g-C 3 N 4 /TiO 2  nanocoating on titanium-based implants to provide photoelectric stimulation for simultaneous bone and nerve regeneration. The integration of rGO augmented charge transport, whereas g-C 3 N 4  and TiO 2  boosted visible-light-driven photoelectrochemical performance via effective charge carrier separation. The nanocoating, when subjected to light irradiation, enhanced the osteogenic differentiation of MC3T3-E1 cells and facilitated neurite outgrowth in PC12 cells, with the most pronounced effect noted in the rGO-containing system. In a coculture model, the augmented release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP) from neural cells further stimulated osteogenic activity, illustrating the potential of photoresponsive nanocoatings for concurrent nerve and bone regeneration [ 170 ]. Halouane et al. synthesized 2-nitrodopamine-functionalized magnetic nanoparticles immobilized on reduced graphene oxide (rGO) for the rapid and selective extraction of  Escherichia coli  from aqueous and serum specimens. The nanocomposite attained a capture effectiveness of up to 99.9% within 30 min, even at minimal bacterial concentrations (1 × 10¹ cfu mL⁻¹). Subsequent functionalization using PEG-modified pyrene units and anti-fimbrial antibodies facilitated the selective targeting of pathogenic  E. coli  strains within complicated biological environments [ 172 ]. Zeng et al. suggested a multifunctional graphene-based nanodrug delivery system for the cure of drug-resistant osteosarcoma. The device was engineered for near-infrared imaging-guided therapy, featuring preferential tumor accumulation and mitochondrial targeting capabilities. It facilitated synergistic photodynamic and photothermal therapy, which has arisen as a potential approach to surmount chemotherapy resistance in osteosarcoma by augmenting therapeutic efficacy at the cellular organelle level [ 15 ]. Shin et al. designed a graphene oxide-based fluorescence sensing system (GOViRA) for the real-time detection of intracellular dengue virus RNA in live cells. The platform comprises a dye-labeled peptide nucleic acid (PNA) probe that is complementary to the DENV genome, together with dextran-coated reduced graphene oxide, which suppresses fluorescence until hybridization with viral RNA reestablishes the signal. This technique facilitated the sensitive and quantitative detection of viral RNA and was subsequently utilized for high-throughput screening of antiviral drugs. This technique discovered ulipristal as a possible inhibitor of DENV infection, demonstrating verified antiviral efficacy both in vitro and in vivo, possibly via inhibiting viral entry into host cells. Graphene-based materials exhibit potent antimicrobial activity through membrane disruption, oxidative stress, and photothermal effects. Darini et al. (2025) reported that graphene sheets embedded with TiO 2  and CaO nanoparticles achieved excellent microbial reduction in wastewater, lowering counts to as low as 3.0–4.85 CFU/mL for E. coli and S. aureus — significantly better than individual metal oxide components [ 220 ].

Materials based on graphene oxide (GO) reveal the potential in many areas including biocompatibility, biosensing, bioimaging, controlled delivery of drugs and genes, tissue engineering, theranostics, and antimicrobial applications. However, a critical analysis uncovers several limitations including GO applications with conflicting results, the ability to scale, and reliability. Compared to unmodified GO, functionalized and reduced GO (rGO) deliver > 90% cell viability, increased loading of therapeutic molecules (up to 65 wt% DOX), enhanced photothermal conversion, and improved targeting of tumors (e.g., rGO@AuNS hybrids give a peak PA signal sustained for > 4 h vs. GO that was not reduced). In the field of biomedicine, comparative studies suggest CHAIE–GO systems yield the lowest limit of detection (LOD) for miRNA at 0.42 pM, the highest level of osteogenic marker upregulation and > 95% wound closure achieved in 15 days was noted for rGO/silk fibroin scaffolds, and the highest capture of E. coli was found for magnetic rGO hybrids (99.9% efficiency).

On the negative side of the cytotoxicity, oxidative stress, and long-term biodistribution studies (contradictory findings for renal clearance vs. accumulation in the liver/spleen) pose major concerns. Variability of oxidation degree, a complex multi-step synthesis, and limited GMP-compliant scalability pose problems for clinical use. GO-based hybrid systems (PEGylated GO, GO–Fe₃O₄, β-CD-GO@MIL-100(Fe)) present the best overall trade-offs for controlled drug delivery, imaging contrast, and mechanical reinforcement. The majority of studies along these lines lack consistent large-scale validation. The most pressing concern for the field of biomedicine is to design production methodologies that are cost-effective in order to validate the results of laboratory.

sections.heading: Conclusion
paragraphs: Drug delivery, bioimaging, and tissue engineering are just a few of the many biomedical domains that have found uses for it due to its mechanical strength, large surface area, and adaptable functional groups like hydroxyl, carboxyl, and epoxy groups. Recent advancements in the functionalization of GO have addressed its previously observed limitations, such as poor solubility and potential cytotoxicity. The reduction of GO to form reduced graphene oxide through non-toxic reducing agents has significantly improved its dispersion in aqueous environments, enhancing its biocompatibility without compromising its structural integrity. GO can interact with biomolecules to improve targeted medication delivery and gene therapy to overcome the constraints of standard drug administration methods. The ability of GO to degrade safely within the human body eliminates concerns regarding the accumulation of non-biodegradable materials, making it suitable for applications such as wound healing and the treatment of chronic conditions, including neurodegenerative diseases like Alzheimer’s. When it comes to smart drug delivery systems, GO has played a key role in enhancing the regulated release of medicinal drugs. Conjugating GO with targeting molecules takes advantage of its surface functional groups, allowing for the targeted delivery of medications to damaged cells, which is a crucial aspect of cancer therapy. Improved therapeutic efficiency and reduced systemic toxicity have been achieved by controlling the release of medications from GO-based carriers, which is affected by environmental factors, including pH. Their application in drug delivery and gene therapy exhibited encouraging outcomes via regulated release mechanisms, high loading efficiency, and targeted distribution. Moreover, their integration into tissue engineering scaffolds enhances mechanical stability, cellular adhesion, proliferation, and regeneration capacity. The antibacterial and antimicrobial properties of these materials render them interesting options for infection-resistant biomedical equipment and coatings.

This review does a great job at demonstrating the potential of GO based nanomaterials for the many branches of medical application. There are, however, some things that are still being developed that we might not be able to account for. Because this is a research review, and not a systematic review, the articles that cited GO based nanomaterials were selectively chosen. This has potential bias. Since this field is growing quickly, we considered literature from early 2024 to 2026, but we are likely missing some recent examples. The majority of research done in this field remains at the design stage, including small and large scale research, and we only have limited first-in-human safety studies. For that reason, we are not able to contribute to the safety or efficacy of this research or predict how it would perform in a real world application. Finally, we are focusing primarily on GO/rGO platforms and we are not including a deep analysis of nanocarriers, especially liposomes, silica nanoparticles, or metallic nanoparticles in this review. These examples show that more systematic reviews and research studies are needed.

sections.heading: Future Aspects
paragraphs: The future of GO in biomedical applications hinges on several critical areas of development:

Although significant efforts have been made in reducing the cytotoxicity of GO, further optimization of its biocompatibility remains a priority. Future research should focus on refining the surface functionalization of GO to achieve minimal immunogenicity and long-term biocompatibility, particularly for in vivo applications. Subsequent research must prioritize elucidating dose-dependent toxicity, biodistribution, immune system activation, degradation kinetics, organ accumulation, and clearance mechanisms in therapeutically applicable contexts. The integration of GO in DDS can be further improved by incorporating smart release mechanisms, such as stimuli-responsive systems that respond to changes in pH, temperature, or enzymatic activity. This approach would allow for highly specific, controlled, and sustained drug release, enhancing therapeutic efficacy while minimizing side effects. Additionally, combining GO with other materials like polymers, liposomes, and nanocarriers could yield hybrid systems with synergistic effects, further advancing the potential for personalized medicine. The incorporation of GO with other imaging agents could improve spatial resolution and tissue penetration, enabling non-invasive in vivo monitoring of disease progression and therapeutic response. A combination of GO with photothermal or photodynamic therapies could offer a powerful tool for treating tumors with high precision while minimizing systemic toxicity. GO’s potential in tissue engineering, particularly in bone and neural regeneration, remains largely unexplored. Future work could focus on developing GO-based scaffolds that promote cell proliferation, differentiation, and tissue integration. By combining GO with growth factors, cytokines, or other biomolecules, it may be possible to create functional tissue constructs for the regeneration of damaged organs and tissues. Clinical translation necessitates enhanced alignment with regulatory frameworks set by entities such as the U.S. Food and Drug Administration and the European Medicines Agency. Subsequent research must include standardized toxicity evaluation methodologies, synthesis methods compliant with Good Manufacturing Practices, validation of sterilizing processes, and testing for shelf-life stability.

In conclusion, while graphene oxide has shown immense promise in the biomedical field, continued research and development are essential to overcoming the challenges related to its toxicity, stability, and functionalization. The future of GO in medicine will likely depend on its integration with other cutting-edge technologies, such as artificial intelligence, nanorobotics, and personalized medicine, to further enhance its capabilities in treating complex diseases.
